body.text: On 19 November, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled by nine votes to six that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya in northern Rakhine State in 2017. This is the first time in the Court’s 80-year history that it has found a state responsible for committing genocide. The Court rejected Myanmar’s argument that its “clearance operations” were acts of counter-terrorism. It ordered restitution and compensation, and gave Myanmar two years to report on measures taken.

For ASEAN, the ruling lands awkwardly; it would affect the grouping’s assessment of Myanmar’s adherence to its Five-Point Consensus more than its approach towards the country. The 49th ASEAN Summit, held in Manila days earlier, maintained the restriction on Myanmar’s representation to non-political representatives, even as some members signalled openness to “calibrated re-engagement” with Myanmar’s post-election administration headed by Mr Min Aung Hlaing. A day before the ruling, he told Parliament he disagreed with recent ASEAN statements made with “full member consensus”, and announced a review of Myanmar’s future engagement with ASEAN. He has since stated that Myanmar would respect the ASEAN Charter.
With the ruling, an ASEAN member state now stands formally responsible for genocide, which sits among the gravest of crimes under international law.

Naypyidaw’s response came on 20 November. Its foreign ministry said the judgment “came as a great disappointment”, stressed that it was not unanimous, and insisted that the 2017 military operations were counter-terrorism actions. It referred to the Rohingya as “Bengalis”, a label widely considered derogatory because it implies they are foreign migrants from Bangladesh. A government spokesperson called the ruling unfair, and cited the China-Russia-US declaration issued in Shenzhen on 19 November, noting that the ICC and “other similar bodies” must not abuse their jurisdiction.

The ICJ’s rulings are binding, but the Court cannot enforce them. Under the UN Charter, The Gambia can ask the Security Council to recommend or decide on measures to operationalise the judgment, but vetoes may constrain action, so any pressure or action may come mainly from individual states. The UK has expelled Myanmar’s defence attaché and summoned its chargé d’affaires. London has since formally recognised the genocide and sanctioned five senior military figures. At the UK’s request and backed by France, the Security Council will meet privately on 7 December. UN human rights chief Volker Türk has urged UN member states to halt transfers of military equipment, jet fuel and dual-use items to Myanmar. Washington was cautious, saying it was studying the decision and warning against politicising the Court, a stance consistent with its opposition to South Africa’s case against Israel. Beijing voiced concern about “jurisdiction overreach”.

The judgment’s legal obligations fall on Myanmar: restitution, compensation and a report within two years. It creates no new obligations for other states. But it settles the factual question, and Genocide Convention parties remain bound by their duty to prevent genocide, which makes military or dual-use support to Myanmar’s armed forces legally riskier. Beyond that, responses are political choices, ranging from the UK’s expulsion of Myanmar’s defence attaché and subsequent targeted sanctions, to Switzerland’s statement that it “expects the parties to comply”. If Myanmar files a report in 2028, it will be a marker of compliance. Whether that report would propose substantive or token measures remains to be seen. Min Aung Hlaing recently stated that Myanmar would address the obligations it deemed necessary (or appropriate) and reject those it does not.

Within ASEAN, seven member states, including Singapore, are parties to the Genocide Convention and retain an existing duty to prevent genocide; Indonesia, Thailand, Brunei and Timor-Leste are not. Before the verdict, Thailand’s foreign minister said he did not expect the ruling to disrupt the proposed calibrated re-engagement approach. After the verdict, he called it a legal matter between Myanmar and the Court that would not derail Bangkok’s engagement. The outgoing Chair, the Philippines, has issued a national statement that may become a template: it stressed that ICJ decisions “must be respected” without explicitly calling on Myanmar to comply. Malaysia has since done likewise.

The ICJ ruling thus gives ASEAN another reference point for its progress-based approach, but also another layer of complexity, as members weigh the ruling differently and Naypyidaw dismisses it as unjust.

Singapore, the incoming Chair, has followed suit: its foreign ministry said it respects the judgment and is studying its implications. It expressed deep concern over the plight of the Rohingya, and reiterated its call for conditions for “safe, voluntary and dignified repatriation of displaced persons”. This is the landscape facing Singapore’s ASEAN Chair year, which formally starts on 1 January 2027. Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said Singapore will continue efforts under the Five-Point Consensus and that “engagement must be two-way”. However, Naypyidaw signalled in August that it saw no need for a Special Envoy under Singapore’s chairmanship.

The ruling may not affect ASEAN’s approach so much as its yardstick. ASEAN has already agreed to limit Myanmar’s representation and pursue progress-based engagement. The question ASEAN faces in 2027 is whether Myanmar’s response to the judgment counts towards that progress. This will be contested: members are not equally bound by the Convention, and some, such as Thailand and Cambodia, are leaning towards re-engagement. The ASEAN Chair may have more leeway to pursue quieter but equally important ways, such as keeping references to international law and conditions in Rakhine State in its statements, and raising the ruling in consultations.

The ruling also bears on ASEAN’s longstanding engagement with Myanmar on the Rohingya issue. Although ASEAN statements avoid the term “Rohingya” at Myanmar’s insistence, they have since 2017 carried paragraphs on Rakhine State, supporting safe and dignified repatriation. ASEAN has also worked with Myanmar on the humanitarian dimension. The bloc has continued to monitor Myanmar’s response to the issue, as well as the aftermath of the 2021 coup and the progress (or lack thereof) in implementing the Five-Point Consensus.

The ruling recognises what the Rohingya have endured and their identity as a distinct group. But recognition alone will not lead to their return to Myanmar. Continued intense fighting between the Arakan Army and the Myanmar armed forces in Rakhine rules out early returns, and Naypyidaw’s pledge to repatriate “as and when situations permit” suggests any return will be on its terms.

The ICJ ruling thus gives ASEAN another reference point for its progress-based approach, but also another layer of complexity, as members weigh the ruling differently and Naypyidaw dismisses it as unjust. Though ASEAN cannot enforce the ruling, it can still decide how much weight to give it.
